it is an area where there can be some confusion. The city's electric base rate is established by the city. That rate supports local electric system that we own and operate. It provides revenue for things such as operations, maintenance, customer service, metering, infrastructure, reliability, capital improvements, and financial obligations.
The power cost adjustment, or PCA, is different. The PCA is a separate pass-through for our wholesale power. It reflects changes in the cost of wholesale electricity used to serve our customers.

It is not city discretionary revenue. It does not fund city staffing, local operations, capital projects, debt, or reserves. So while the base rate and PCA appear together on a customer electric bill, they serve two different purposes.

The city establishes the base rate, the PCA reflects wholesale power changes, excuse me. And with that, I'm going to go into our presentation. Today, I want to walk through why the utility rates are structured the way they are, and more importantly, what those rates are intended to support.

There are really two different issues, again, the city base and the cost for wholesale power, PCA. The goal is to make sure we're funding today's operations while also preparing for future capital needs and maintaining appropriate financial reserves.

Then we've got the base rate versus pass-through. This is probably the most important distinction in this presentation. The base rate is established by the city, again, supports local utility systems, operation maintenance, customer service, and such.
The PCA, while it appears on the customer's electric bill, is a pass-through of wholesale electricity. It is determined, or it is built to us by Dominion Virginia Power starting in May.
There were a couple of years ago, in 2022, we actually had two rate increases for the PCA in May and November. So that hasn't happened because we see a big increase.
What is the PCA? The PCA is important because it can change independently of the city's annual rate settings. PCA reflects changes in the cost of wholesale electricity used to serve our customers.
It takes effect in May each year, and changes in wholesale power cost flows through the customers. The key point I want council and our residents to understand is the city controls the base rate.
Wholesale is separate, and it's provided, again, by Dominion. That distinction becomes particularly important when we're talking about changes customers have seen as of recent on their bills.
The rate strategy did not come from simply looking at just one year of expenses. Nugen, an independent contractor, conducted a review of the utility funds and recommended a multi-year strategy.

The objective was to align recurring revenue with recurring costs, address financial pressure, rebuild reserves, and provide funding for capital programs. Council's FY27 actions reflected that strategy.
10.5% increase in electric, 25% in water, and 3% in sewer. In dollars and cents, for 1,000 kilowatts in electric, that would have been a $12 increase a month.
We're in water for 5,000 gallons, $7.72. And in SOAR, the bill would have increased by 81 cents for 5,000 gallons. So on the city side, city rates would have been $20.53.

So those five years, we're kind of trying to make up for. What do our electric rates support? Well, again, our base rates support everything that is happening in the city.
It's paying for our debt service. It's paying for capital improvement. It's paying for the infrastructure replacements. All of that is part of the rate that the city approves. Water.
Water has the largest financial gap. The projected water fund shortfall, as discussed during the FY27, was approximately $4 to $4.7 million. Water is also extremely capital intensive.

We have our own water treatment plant. We've got storage. We've got aging infrastructure. So we continuously need to invest. The 25% adjustment is intended to move the fund toward a more sustainable financial position, rather than continuing to rely on short-term solutions.

Why water reserves matter. I want to clarify the negative pooled cash number because it can be misunderstood. The city uses a centralized pooled cash structure. A negative fund balance position does not mean the city cannot pay its bills.

It means the water fund has drawn more from the pooled cash structure than it has contributed. The rate strategy is intended to help restore that fund to a sustainable financial position. On the SOAR, SOAR is our strongest one.
The 3% is basically inflationary, just to be able to keep up with everything. So financially, that is the best fund. What happens if rates do not keep pace?

Well, the slide is really about where the cost goes if it isn't recovered through rate. The cost does not disappear. We either defer capital projects, use reserves, increase rates more significantly in the future, or reduce the level of service investment.
It's simple. We have to have that base, a sustainable rate strategy. A healthy utility system requires these pieces to work together. Revenue, operations, capital investment, and reserves.

If one of those pieces falls behind, eventually the others have to compensate. The objective of the current strategy is to keep those four pieces moving together. For electric, that means maintaining the local system through the base rate while separately passing through wholesale power costs.

For water, it means addressing the largest financial gap. For sewer, it means maintaining a sustainable path without creating a larger correction. In closing, the overall message is that utility rates are not simply about this year's operating budget.

They're about maintaining reliable service today, replacing infrastructure when it is needed, preparing for future demands, and maintaining enough financial capacity to respond when unexpected costs occur. The RAID strategy is intended to address those needs through predictable recurring revenue rather than deferring the costs into the future.
